1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5.strategy: Joins the knight in attacking f7, so Black has to answer the threat at once. White keeps the initiative in an open, tactical game where the gambit pawn is traded for activity; it leads to the line treated as the main one of the whole gambit.

Backs up the knight and clears the c1 bishop's path to f4, so White threatens to win the gambit pawn back at once. A kicked knight can also retreat to d3 without blocking the d-pawn; White builds a central base and keeps attacking.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Kieseritzky Gambit, Berlin Defence, Rubinstein Variation

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5.strategy: Takes the g-pawn at once and levels the material, but leaves e4 undefended, so Black takes it with a lead in development. White then has to steer into forcing, rather drawish complications or risks staying a pawn down.

The only sensible way to meet the threat on f7: the pawn closes the bishop's diagonal and attacks the bishop. After the exchange, material is level and White's bishop is blocked by its own pawn, so the fight moves to the centre and the open lines around the kings.

Counterstrikes in the centre instead of grabbing e4: the pawn opens the c8 bishop against the knight on g4 and adds to the pressure on e4. White's knight is attacked twice and has to trade itself off, leaving Black with the better development.
